Hypothesis tested first: the orchestrating assistant called plugin AGENTS directly and never invoked plugin SKILLS, so the skill pipelines that spawn the other agents never ran.

## Method

- Transcripts: `~/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-orin-dx/b8d16e96-....jsonl` (36,217 lines, 29 Sep to 3 Oct) and `~/.claude/projects/-Users-gabe-Projects-pages/24655582-....jsonl` (63,262 lines, 8 to 16 Oct). Line numbers below are 1-based transcript lines. Streamed with `python3 -I` scripts; no file was read whole.
- Listed every `Skill` tool_use, every `<command-name>` slash command, and every `Agent` tool_use by `subagent_type` in both sessions. Counted Skill calls across all 812 transcripts of the orin-dx and pages project dirs (`rows.json`).
- Read the `skill_listing` and `agent_listing_delta` attachments at session start, the user prompts asking for plugins, and the assistant's next actions.
- Compared against `plugins/smith/skills/implement/SKILL.md`, `plugins/sentinel/skills/gate/SKILL.md`, `plugins/scribe/skills/*/SKILL.md`, and the existing digests (`B-orin-dx-sessions.md`, `C-pages-sessions.md`, `D-outcomes.md` in the job tmp dir).
- Limit: the assistant's thinking blocks are empty in the transcripts, so its reasons are inferred from visible text and actions, not read.

## Findings

| # | Finding | Count | Refs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Skill` calls, orin-dx session | 0 | whole file |
| 2 | `Skill` calls, pages session | 4: `artifact-design`, `muse:component`, `artifact-capabilities`, `workflow-authoring`. One plugin skill. | pages 3354, 11906, 14968, 21679 |
| 3 | Slash commands | orin: `/effort /fork /exit /model /login`; pages: `/remote-control`. No plugin command. | orin 8, 18920, 20533 |
| 4 | Plugin skill calls across all 812 transcripts in both projects | 7 `Skill` calls in 4 files. Plugin ones: `muse:component` (1), `scribe:gate-spec` (1, inside one subagent file), `vanguard:research` (1, a blog session). `smith:implement`, `navigator:plan`, `sentinel:gate`, `scribe:draft-spec`, `scribe:verify-spec` are never invoked. | rows.json |
| 5 | Skills were available | Yes. Listings of 60 and 61 skills at session start include `muse:component`, `navigator:plan`, `smith:implement`, `sentinel:gate` and all scribe skills. Not truncated. | orin 18, pages 16 |
| 6 | Agents were also listed, each described "Delegate to this subagent when...", including `smith:reviewer`, `smith:mutator`, `sentinel:*` | Direct delegation was always a legal and visible path. | orin 16, pages 14 |
| 7 | Agent calls, orin-dx | `muse:exit-gate` 28, `fork` 26, `muse:drafter` 25, `general-purpose` 18, `smith:implementer` 17, `scribe:exit-gate` 10, `scribe:drafter` 7, `navigator:planner` 3, `navigator:challenger` 3, `muse:auditor` 1 | scan |
| 8 | Agent calls, pages | `muse:exit-gate` 51, untyped fork/teammate 41, `general-purpose` 24, `smith:implementer` 18, `fork` 14, `muse:auditor` 9, `muse:drafter` 8, `scribe:drafter` 3, `scribe:auditor` 3, `navigator:planner` 1, `navigator:challenger` 1 | scan |
| 9 | Trigger prompt, orin 20776 (30 Sep): "Not DocNav then... Do we make these proper react components? Use our plugins for quality work" | Next: Bash `ls`/`cat README.md` in `~/Projects/agent-plugins` (20789-20791), then "build SiteNav using the Muse->Navigator->Smith pipeline" and `Agent muse:drafter` (20797-20798). No `Skill` call. | orin 20776-20798 |
| 10 | The assistant framed plugins as agent personas | "Muse specs..., Navigator plans..., and Smith builds it" (20942). Pages: "After that, Navigator plans, Smith builds with tests, and Sentinel gates" (14940). Sentinel was promised and never ran. | orin 20942, pages 14940 |
| 11 | No explanation for skipping skills | No assistant text in either session mentions skipping a skill, `reviewer`, `mutator` or `sentinel`. | text search of both sessions |
| 12 | When the skill was loaded, the whole pipeline ran | Pages 11905: "I'm loading the component skill so I follow its exact pipeline." Then 8 drafts, 9 audits, 51 gate calls. No unused muse agent in pages. | pages 11905-14898 |
| 13 | Smith steps in some other form | Reviewer/recon/exit-gate equivalents: none (no Agent call is described as review, verify or gate of implementation). Mutation: partly inline, since implementers report "temporary mutations, restored" and discrimination checks. Verification otherwise relied on `just check`, Playwright e2e and the orchestrator's own checks. | orin 28037, 28057, 28074, 28098, 28305; pages 21361 |

### Why exactly these agents

| Unused agent | Where the plugin puts it | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| `smith:recon`, `reviewer`, `mutator`, `exit-gate` | Only inside `smith:implement` (recon, implementer, mutator, reviewer, exit-gate). | Skill never invoked; `implementer` called alone per task (35 times). |
| `sentinel:recon/verifier/exit-gate` | Only inside `sentinel:gate`. | Skill never invoked; no other path leads there. |
| `scribe:verifier` | Separate skill `scribe:verify-spec`, a distinct step between `draft-spec` and `audit-spec`. | Assistant called `scribe:drafter` then `scribe:exit-gate` directly (orin 26597, 26723). |
| `scribe:arch-auditor` | Separate skill `scribe:audit-architecture`. | Same skip. |
| Used: `muse:*` | All three agents in one skill, `muse:component`. | Skill loaded in pages. In orin the agents were called directly, and `muse:auditor` ran only once. |
| Used: `navigator:*`, `scribe:drafter/exit-gate`, `smith:implementer` | Self-contained "do one thing" agents whose descriptions read as direct delegation targets. | Called directly as personas. |

The unused agents are those reachable only through a skill that was never invoked, or through a skipped step of the scribe chain. The used agents are those an orchestrator can pick from the agent list without a skill.

## Verdict on the hypothesis: PARTLY CONFIRMED (mostly confirmed)

Confirmed:
- Orin has 0 `Skill` calls in 36k lines. Pages has 1 plugin skill call in 63k lines. The pipelines were hand-composed from agents.
- The never-used agents are exactly those gated behind the uninvoked skills (`smith:implement`, `sentinel:gate`) or behind skipped steps of the scribe chain.
- The one plugin skill that was loaded (`muse:component`) ran its full pipeline.

Qualified:
- "Skills unavailable" is refuted: they were listed in both sessions.
- Skipping skills is not the whole cause. `muse:*` also ran directly in orin. The shared cause is that the assistant treated plugins as a cast of agents (Muse, Navigator, Smith, Sentinel) and sequenced them itself, a habit the agent descriptions invite.
- Whether cost or stalls drove the omission of reviewer/mutator is not shown. The digests record 17 failed agent tasks and many "stalled" streams, and a repo-wide pre-commit gate that "cost me about a dozen waits" (pages 21361), but no assistant text links these to skipping. Treat as unknown.
- Later, the user directed less ceremony (pages 49946, 14 Oct: "lean less on the specs and tests"). That explains the dropped gates after 14 Oct, not the earlier skipped Smith steps.

## Impact (only where evidence supports it)

- No implementation review, independent exit-gate verdict or baseline recon ever ran on `smith:implementer` output. Verdicts came from the implementers themselves and the orchestrator.
- Defects were found after the fact by human-directed review or late e2e rather than by a plugin gate (D-outcomes.md items 1, 2, 7, 8):
  - Orin 3 Oct review (36196): "the tests assert markup, so all 29 twx tests pass with every defect below present". This is the weakness `smith:mutator` survivor analysis targets. Caveat: the code reviewed was Codex's, not `smith:implementer`'s, so it shows the pattern, not a Smith miss.
  - SiteNav logo-cap regression (AC-112, AC-017) was caught only by a manual `just e2e` run (orin 36113-36143); Playwright is `runInCI: false`.
  - Pages: spec/code drift at the 760px boundary, where 296 nav-fixture tests pinned the wrong constant (D-outcomes item 2); contrast and target-size defects found by the first automated suite four days after base specs passed (item 7); e2e work surfaced 6 product defects and two were "fixed as spec exemptions" by changing the spec (C-pages-sessions, pages ~21276).
- Not supported: that `smith:reviewer`, `mutator` or `exit-gate` would have caught these. The evidence shows a verification gap those agents are designed for (test discrimination, sibling and family search, current-state check), not a demonstrated catch.
- The spec side also skipped `verify-spec` and `audit-architecture`. Drift between SPEC-001/003a/003c and shipped code (D-outcomes item 1) is what `audit-architecture` and `spec-drift` target; again plausible, not shown. The drafting gates that did run produced many real blockers (118 across re-gates, pages 22772), so spec quality was not neglected overall.

## Recommendations

1. Make skills the entry point. State in the harness instructions and each plugin README: "For plugin work, call the plugin's Skill; call its agents directly only when the skill says so." The skills already hold order, retry limits and routing that the orchestrator re-derived by hand.
2. Rewrite agent descriptions that read "Delegate to this subagent when..." to mark skill-internal steps: "Step N of `smith:implement`; do not call alone". Prioritize `smith:implementer`, `navigator:*`, `scribe:drafter/exit-gate`, the agents actually called directly. Hide internal agents from the model-visible agent list if the harness allows.
3. Fold the scribe chain (draft, verify, audit, architecture, gate) into one pipeline skill with optional steps marked, like `muse:component` and `sentinel:gate`. Today `verifier` and `arch-auditor` sit behind separate skills that nothing triggers.
4. Add a router skill mapping intent to pipeline: component spec -> `muse:component`; plan -> `navigator:plan`; implement -> `smith:implement`; "use our plugins" / "quality work" -> the lifecycle in order, ending at `sentinel:gate`. The prompt at orin 20776 matched no skill trigger phrase.
5. In `smith:implement`, forbid calling `smith:implementer` alone. If cost or stalls are the real barrier, define an explicit light mode (recon and exit-gate only) instead of letting steps drop silently.
6. Make skipping visible: the pipeline's final artifact should list which gates ran and which were skipped, so "Sentinel gates" cannot be promised (pages 14940) and then silently dropped.
7. Add a `mason:evaluate` check for the pattern: a smith agent call with no `smith:implement` Skill call, or a spec exit-gate with no preceding verify/audit.
8. Log plugin skill and agent use per session (the `rows.json` scan is enough) so non-use is observable without manual investigation.

4

6	
7	Each run used `claude -p --model claude-sonnet-5-5 --plugin-dir <plugin under test> --no-session-persistence` in a throwaway project directory outside `~/.claude` (a directory under it is treated as sensitive and blocks writes), with a budget cap and `--permission-mode acceptEdits` or `auto`. The prompt was a plain request, never naming the skill. Artifacts were validated against the real schemas with `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`. The throwaway directories were deleted afterwards, so only the numbers and findings below are kept.
8	
9	## Runs
10	
11	| # | Skill | Request | Result | Cost |
12	| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
13	| 1 | `sketch` | "Show me some options for the hero section", brand file given, no direction | Wrote a brief with stated assumptions, proposed four distinct named directions, asked two optional questions (the skill allows three), and stopped for a pick. Did not open with the mode line | $0.14 |
14	| 2 | `sketch` | Same, direction chosen, inside `~/.claude` | Every write was blocked as a sensitive path; it said so, did not try another location, planned three structurally different options and ended with the skipped-gates line | $0.21 |
15	| 3 | `sketch` | Same, direction chosen, temporary directory | Opened with the mode line, said no render was seen, built three static pages and a board, and wrote a record that **failed the schema with 22 violations**: it could not read the schema file and followed the skill's loose prose (wrong id formats, wrong field names, missing required fields) | $0.25 |
16	| 4 | `sketch` | Same prompt after the record shape was added inline to the skill | Opened with the mode line, same honesty about renders, and the record **validated with zero errors** | $0.22 |
17	| 5 | `spike` | "Can we rely on the standard library alone for an exact Wilcoxon p-value for about 30 pairs?" | Opened with the mode line, ran real code, caught a bug in its own first version by brute-force checking, listed what was verified and what was not (including that scipy was absent), wrote only to scratch; the `spike-report@1` **validated with zero errors** | $0.18 |
18	| 6 | `promote` | A decided sketch fixture (valid against `option-set@1`), "promote the chosen option" | Wrote a `requirement@1` that **validated with zero errors**: eight `done_when` items including a labeled owner review of the approved render, unverified items carried forward as conditions to confirm, rejected and parked options in `out_of_scope` with their reasons quoted, the decision reason copied word for word; named the next stage without starting it | $0.15 |
19	| 7 | `explorer` | A delegation packet for one option | One `muse:explorer` subagent ran, built and rendered its option under the scratch path, differentiated it from the named siblings, flagged that the mobile render was captured but not viewed, and returned an `option-set@1` that **validated with zero errors** | $0.33 |
20	
21	Total about $1.49.
22	
23	## What changed because of the pilots
24	
25	- **Schema files are not reliably readable at run time**, so each skill now carries the record or report shape inline, with the required fields and id formats (22 violations became 0 on the same prompt; one run each). The same limit applies to every existing skill that points at `shared/schemas/...`; whether the references resolve after install is WP-621.
26	- **The mode line** is now an explicit instruction in the first workflow step. Runs 4 and 5 opened with it; run 1 did not.
27	- **The board preview frames were clipped** in the page the model built, hiding the diagrams; the skill now says to make frames at least 640px tall and let the board scroll.
28	- **The explorer used absolute paths and the `file` kind for screenshots**; its output rules now ask for workspace-relative paths and the `screenshot` kind. This change was not re-run.
29	
30	## What the pilots do not show
31	
32	- One run per scenario on one model; the variation between runs is unknown.
33	- They ran headless, so the user's direction pick and the decision round were supplied by the prompt, not by a person choosing from the board.
34	- Nothing measured whether exploration is faster or produces fewer defects found later than the ad hoc work it replaces; that needs the paired design in `docs/evaluation-methodology.md`.
35	- The sketch pilots had no browser permission and fell back to the documented "not rendered" path; only the explorer rendered. The rendered quality of the options was seen once, on a board from run 4: three structurally different layouts with placeholder copy, with the diagram previews clipped (now addressed).
36	- `spike` pointed at `smith/implement` and not `muse/promote` for the next step because only the `smith` plugin was loaded.
37	- The Codex counterparts were not run; they are checked only by the repository's native-source tests.

# Wave 0 implementation log

Status as of 2026-10-20 on branch `worktree-frontend-design-evaluation`. Five of the Wave 0 work packages in `CATALOG.md` are started or done. Nothing is released: no plugin version, changelog or tag changed (see "Release bookkeeping").

| WP | Status | What changed | Verified by |
| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
| WP-617 Codex model ids | Done | `harnesses/codex/agent-roles/README.md` names `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-6.1-sol` and `gpt-6-astra` (the selectable models on the Codex models page, 2026-10-20), notes that effort labels are relative and the tiers are unevaluated; generated `dist/codex` copies regenerated | `just marketplace-check`; no `gpt-5.6` or `terra` left in `dist`, `harnesses` or `.agents` |
| WP-620 Claude manifests | Done | `tools/sync-claude-manifests.py` generates `plugins/<id>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (name, version, description, author) from each `plugin.json`, with `--check`; `just claude-manifests` is in `just check` and CI; `just claude-validate` runs `claude plugin validate --strict` on every plugin and the marketplace | `just claude-validate`: 10 plugins and the marketplace pass `--strict`, and validation now reads each manifest (before, the directory form checked nothing) |
| WP-622 AGY and root marketplace | Partly done | Removed the dead `$schema` URL (404) from the root `marketplace.json`; nothing in tests, scripts or CI read it | `just check` |
| WP-624 Hook validator spike | Done, registered | `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, a `PreToolUse` hook on `SubagentHandback` that checks exit-gate handbacks against their verdict schema, denies with the errors, caps denials at 3 per agent, enforces the retry cap in the report, and fails open; registered by `hooks/hooks.json` in muse, scribe, smith, sentinel and ranger (ADR 012) | `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (13 tests) and a live run and `verification/scripts/handback-conformance.py` over 45 recorded verdicts |
| WP-01 and WP-02 `muse` fixes | Done | The `muse` docs no longer point to a ranger accessibility taxonomy that does not exist (`plugin.json`, README, `SKILL.md`, root `marketplace.json`); the `muse` exit-gate produces `verdict@3` (agent, skill, README, `plugin.json`, Codex skill and catalog, root README table); `verdict@1` has no producer and is kept unchanged | `just check` (66 tests); `just marketplace-check`; validator tests for `muse` routing and for escalation as a blocker |
| WP-625 Reasoning-wording lint | Done | `tests/test_reasoning_wording.py` fails on text that demands reproduced reasoning (verbatim, step-by-step, chain of thought), with one documented exception for the immutable `requirement@1` schema | Passes; fails when the probe's demand is planted in an agent file |

## What the work found

- **`claude plugin validate plugins/<id>` was a false pass** because the manifests sit at the plugin root. With the generated `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` it validates the manifest, and the repo-only keys (`id`, `consumes`, `produces`) stay in `plugin.json` where Claude Code ignores them.
- **Recorded gate verdicts nearly all conform to their schemas.** 33 of 45 conform; all 12 violations are `verdict_summary` over 300 characters (`VERIFY-3.md` section 5). A hook would have asked for one trim on about 27% of handbacks.
- **`muse` gates mostly emitted `verdict@3`-shaped output** (26 of 36; the other 9 of the 45 files are `scribe` gates) while `muse` documented `verdict@1`, and its prompt told the agent to set `verdict` to `"escalate"`, which no schema allows. WP-02 (done) moved `muse` to `verdict@3` and made escalation an `escalation_required` blocker, as in the other four gates; the validator now checks `muse` against `verdict@3` only.
- **A bug in the validator was found only by real data:** a schema property with a list of types (`["string", "null"]`). It is fixed and has a regression test.
- **The `requirement@1` schema describes `reasoning` as "chain-of-thought during capture".** It is immutable (ADR 004), agents reach it through a file read and not a prompt, so the lint carries a documented exception; a future `requirement@2` should use the "private scratchpad" wording.

## Open items from this work

- The README documents AGY installs through the community `agy-plugins-cli`. Fetched source snippets suggest that tool discovers plugins as top-level repository directories, which would not find plugins under `plugins/`. This is unverified; test an install in an isolated environment before changing the README (WP-622, WP-621).

## Courier changeset guidance (Callisto request)

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `changeset@2` capped the summary at 200 characters and the agent, skill and schema repeated one-clause and one-sentence limits, so a limit users will hit went into the unforwarded `reasoning` | New `changeset@3` (no cap, Markdown, `disposition` of new, update-existing or none) and `release-artifact@3`; `changeset@2` and `release-artifact@2` are untouched per ADR 004 | `tests/test_changeset_schema.py` |
| The agent worked per diff topic, with no way to update an entry or say none is needed | Outcome-level granularity and `disposition` in the agent, skills and Codex counterparts | Live run below |
| The Semver table had no rows for a CLI's flags, output, exit codes or serialized files | Rows added to `shared/references/delivery/changesets.md`, with an entry-shape section and a bad-versus-good pair (117 lines of the 120 cap) | `just check` |
| Claude sessions wrote changesets, commits and PR text freehand | The `changeset`, `commit` and `pr` skill descriptions now say to use the skill instead, and the courier README says when to use each; no hook | Tests on the descriptions |
| Courier moved to 3.1.0 with changelog | `plugin.json`, README, CHANGELOG, marketplace and Codex manifest agree | `just versions` |

Live run: `courier:changeset-analyzer` on `gh pr diff 483 --repo orin-dx/callisto` (24.9 kB), one run on Sonnet 5.5. It returned one `new` entry for one outcome: a lead line on the link, then what you see and where, the limit that a changeset pushed straight to the branch gets no link, the optional `pr` field for scripts, and that upgrading needs no action. It classified the change as a minor new capability. It did not write the "why it helps" as a separate bullet but put it in the lead line.

**Finding: `shared/...` reference paths depend on the working directory.** In that run the agent reported it could not find `shared/references/delivery/changesets.md` and fell back to the schema-implied rules. The agent was started from a directory outside the plugin, and its `load_first` paths are relative to the plugin root, not to where the agent runs. This is separate from, and in addition to, the dangling-symlink install defect fixed in the marketplace sources (VERIFY-3 section 7): even a correct install leaves a relative `shared/...` path unresolvable from a user's project. It likely explains the pilots where schema files were not readable at run time. Not fixed here. Options: pass the plugin root into the skill and agent instructions if the host substitutes it, name the references in the skill body so they load with it, or inline the few rules an agent cannot work without. Needs a host check first.

`pr-narrator` and `commit-analyzer` were then changed to match: they follow the repository's own conventions (a pull request template, recent commit scopes and subject style), keep limits in the body instead of the scratchpad, mark breaking changes to command output, exit codes and file formats, and the narrator names or recommends a changeset. One live run of both on the same PR 483 diff: the PR body followed the template sections, put four limits under a "Limits a reader will hit" list, said the tests were not run and gave commands, and added a Changeset section. Two weaknesses: the narrator stated an inferred behavior (shallow clones give no link and no error) as fact while its scratchpad called it an inference, which a new rule now forbids; and the haiku commit body described the mechanism and omitted the direct-push limit, which is not fixed (a commit body is short and the limit belongs in the changeset and PR). Both agents again could not find their `shared/` reference, the working-directory finding above.

Not done: changes in the Callisto repo (its AGENTS.md or PR template), which are recommendations only: say in its AGENTS.md to invoke `courier/changeset` for changesets and `courier/pr` for PR text, and add a changeset prompt to its PR template.

| Finding | Action | Evidence |

Muse `sketch` and `promote` descriptions cut to 450 characters or fewer. Four READMEs gained one "about to do it by hand" line | `tests/test_skill_routing.py` |

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `planner` wrote exact code for every task that `implementer` may discard and `challenger` policed; `plan@1` does not require code (only `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps`, `commit_message`) | No schema change. `planner` now states outcome, files, signatures, proving tests with assertions, verification command, commit message and `covers_criteria`, with code only for non-obvious or costly-to-reshape logic; `challenger` flags full bodies for routine logic and no longer treats absent code as a defect; Claude and Codex skills and the README updated. ADR 014 supersedes ADR 009's every-task code requirement only | `tests/test_navigator_plan.py`; `just check` |

Measured once each (Sonnet 5.5, a two-task, six-criterion Python fixture with the schema path given in the prompt): the old planner wrote 9,777 characters (8 steps, 18 function definitions); the new one wrote 5,578 (18 steps, 1 definition). Both validated against `plan@1` and covered all six criteria. One run each is weak evidence on one small fixture. Not tested: whether implementers do better or worse from the smaller plans, and the challenger on either shape.

**Finding: without the schema in reach, the planner invents fields.** A first pair of runs started from a directory with no `shared/schemas` and both wrote task keys the schema forbids (`outcome`, `approach`, `tests`, `verify_command`), the same working-directory problem as the courier finding above. The planner now says to add no keys outside the schema and to carry the content in `steps`; the final runs also named the schema path in the prompt.

Not done: the `plan@1` field descriptions still say "exact code" (a published schema is not edited, ADR 004); a `plan@2` with explicit outcome, signature and test fields is deferred.

## Gate rounds (track B, ADR 013)

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Every spec failed its first gate and blocker counts were non-monotonic (SPEC-001: 18, 5, 6, 0, 0, 2, 0, 6, 2, 3, 2, 8, 3) | Each of the five exit gates now states two output rules, worded the same: round one lists the complete blocker set; a retry cites only unresolved prior blockers or regressions the fix introduced, and any other new issue is a non-blocking `coverage_gaps` entry; every blocker names the criterion, cites quoted text or a location and states the exact change; wording or style issues are notes | `just check` exit 0; `verdict@3` unchanged |
| Drafters sent unchecked drafts to the gate | New `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` (blocker shape, rounds, spec checklist) loaded by `muse:drafter` and `scribe:drafter`, with a short inline fallback if the path does not resolve; Codex `author` and `judge` role cards updated | `just check` |
| Blocker shape could not be enforced deterministically without false denials | The hook denies only a blocker or coverage gap whose text is whitespace; evidence citing is not checked | `tests/test_handback_validator.py` |

Live runs, one run each on Sonnet 5.5 (Claude Code 2.1.311, `claude -p --permission-mode auto --plugin-dir`, working directory outside the repository, `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` set). The prompt read a task file asking for one delegation to `<plugin>:exit-gate` with a small spec or finding that had known defects. The trace showed `agent_type` `<plugin>:exit-gate` in all four. Scribe, sentinel and smith were accepted on the first report. Ranger was denied once and accepted on the second; the trace does not record the denial reason, so what the first report broke is unknown. All four returned fail with blockers that gave a criterion or finding id, a location and an exact change; the smith report also listed `missing_mutation_gate` and `unresolved_review` as blockers, and the scribe report flagged the TBD and the vague "gracefully" criterion. These runs were round one only: they confirm the hook fires and the gates produce evidence-citing blockers, not that rounds fall. Nothing here measures the retry rule.

Not done: a measured comparison of round counts before and after (needs a paired run of gate, fix and regate, WP-60); passing the prior round's blockers into the gate on retry (the skills do not, so the retry rule depends on the orchestrator); a self-check for `smith:implementer`, `sentinel:verifier` and `ranger` producers; a check that the `shared/...` path resolves from a user's project (see the Courier finding above).

## Integration, path resolution and versions

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Relative `shared/...` paths in agents and skills do not resolve reliably: with `shared` a symlink, a probe skill first tried its own directory and a probe agent first tried the working directory, each costing a failed read; an explicit `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/...` path read on the first try in both | Rewrote 163 references in 66 agent and skill files to the plugin-root form. Codex sources are unchanged because Codex does not substitute the token | Four probe runs (one each, Claude Code 2.1.311, Sonnet 5.5); then `courier:changeset-analyzer` on the Callisto PR 483 diff reported its reference loaded from the full plugin path on the first read |

Limits: the path finding rests on single probe runs; Antigravity's handling of `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in skill and agent text was not tested, and its format shares the authored tree, so confirm it before releasing. The hook-only plugins (sentinel, ranger) are patch bumps although a gate can now deny a report that used to pass; scribe is a minor because its drafter and skills also changed behavior.

## Top-tier models removed

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Two agents (`scribe:arch-auditor`, `scribe:architect`) ran on `claude-fable-5-1`, about twice Opus, and `arch-auditor` runs on every spec; the Codex `judge` role ran on `gpt-6-astra`. The constitution said fable was never for gates or per-finding loops, and no measurement shows either tier catches more | Both scribe agents move to `opus / high`, the constitution drops the fable tier, the Codex `judge` moves to `gpt-6.1-sol / high`; tier tests updated | `just check`. Quality effect unmeasured: run the spec-gating paired comparison in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md` and restore a tier if boundary conflicts or binding verdicts are missed |

Codex `author` role: moved from `gpt-6.1-sol` / high to `gpt-6.1-terra` / medium (Terra is about half of Sol's price per token and is positioned for clear writing; the page lists no effort levels for it, so the effort label stays relative). Other roles unchanged. Unmeasured: whether Terra drafts specs, PR text and changesets as well as Sol; run the spec-drafting and courier comparisons in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md`.

## Model and effort fit

Audit of all 45 agents against the constitution's tiers (haiku/low for mechanical work, sonnet/medium for analysis and execution, opus/high for binding judgment). Two clear mismatches changed: `courier:release-summarizer` sonnet/medium to haiku/low (deterministic aggregation), `scribe:drift-checker` opus/high to sonnet/medium (a diagnostic, not a gate). Left alone pending measurement, in order of likely saving: `ranger:adversary` (one opus call per candidate), `scribe:arch-auditor` (opus on every spec), `sentinel:exit-gate` (maps a verifier report to a verdict without re-reading evidence, so it may not need opus), and whether opus gates need `high` rather than the default effort. Gate quality decides retry rounds, so a cheaper gate that misses more can cost more than it saves; test with the spec-gating comparison in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md` before changing them.

1	# Architecture assumptions register
2	
3	Every part of a harness encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do on its own, and those assumptions go stale as models and hosts change. This register records each load-bearing assumption in `ARCHITECTURE.md` and the decision records, the evidence for and against it, and the check that would retire it. Review it when a new model generation ships, when Claude Code or Codex changes how agents, hooks or plugins work, and before a release. First version: 2026-10-20, from `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/ARCHITECTURE-REVIEW.md` after primary-source verification.
4	
5	Status: **Holds**, **Changing** (a work package is in progress), **Open** (evidence is mixed; a measurement is planned), **Retire** (evidence says drop it).
6	
7	| # | Assumption | Where it lives | Evidence now | Status | Next check |
8	| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
9	| 1 | Context is scarce, so load references on demand | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 1, `<load_first>` blocks | Skills are progressive disclosure natively; Anthropic's context guidance asks for the minimal sufficient information | Holds | Re-read when context-window or compaction behavior changes |
10	| 2 | One agent per cognitive mode | ADR 003, `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 7 | Anthropic recommends splitting by context isolation, not role, and multi-agent runs cost 3 to 15 times a single agent; verifier, adversary and recon splits are justified by independent context | Open | WP-605 classifies each of the 44 agents; WP-601 tests collapsed variants against a no-plugin baseline |
11	| 3 | A byte-identical constitution block is a shared cache prefix | ADR 006 | The block is 6 lines in each agent, so its cost is small; cache prefixes are shared only for the same model, effort, agent type, tools, schema and directory, with a 5-minute subagent TTL | Open | WP-604 measures sharing; no change unless a net benefit is shown |
12	| 4 | Capability tiers by model and effort | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 5 | Effort is a native per-agent control; defaults and semantics differ by model; the Codex tiers were re-chosen by position and are unevaluated | Open | WP-63 sweeps effort at the effort actually run; re-check on each model release |
13	| 5 | JSON schemas are the inter-agent contract | ADR 004 | Portable across harnesses; recorded gate verdicts conform except one rule (summary length) | Holds | Enforce deterministically (WP-602) |
14	| 6 | The `reasoning` scratchpad field is safe | Constitution, 29 of 31 schemas | Documentation names such a field as a refusal trigger; a live probe on Sonnet 5.5 completed normally with the field and refused only a demand for verbatim reasoning; no refusals in 72k+ transcript messages | Holds | `tests/test_reasoning_wording.py` guards the wording; re-run the probe per model generation and on Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Haiku 5.5 (WP-625) |
15	| 7 | Default-fail gates with a retry cap of 3 and human escalation | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 6 | The cap lived in a prompt and was not enforced: eight specs passed with `retry_count` 4 to 9; the `muse` gate told the agent to emit a verdict value no schema allows (fixed) | Changing | WP-602: enforced by a hook in the five gate plugins (ADR 012, live-run once on `muse:exit-gate`); a workflow script may replace the cap check (WP-603) |
16	| 8 | Orchestration is a skill prompt that spawns subagents | Plugin skills | The assistant never invoked the skills (7 Skill calls in 812 transcripts), so agents reachable only through skills never ran; the platform offers workflow scripts that keep state outside the model | Changing | WP-603; Wave 1 makes skills the entry point |
17	| 9 | Work is a sequential pipeline of ten plugins | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 3 | Autonomous runs are getting longer and stage granularity tuned for short horizons goes stale; stages should be elidable | Open | WP-608, WP-18 (mode router) |
18	| 10 | Plans carry exact implementation code | navigator, ADR 009 | Anthropic kept its own planner at high-level design and says over-prescriptive guidance degrades newer models; large plans stalled agents | Open | WP-608: outcome-level plans |
19	| 11 | Verification evidence is text, code and tests | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 4 | Every target harness has a native browser; one study found 44.5% of agent runs never looked at the design screenshots; visible defects shipped past every gate | Changing | WP-607, WP-40, WP-41 |
20	| 12 | Agents are stateless across sessions | no memory design | Decisions were lost between sessions; native memory, persistent plugin data and session search exist | Changing | WP-612, WP-13 |
21	| 13 | Two source trees, one lifecycle contract | `ARCHITECTURE.md` sections 8 to 10 | Codex has its own native plugin format set up in `harnesses/codex/`; Antigravity's format is similar to Claude Code's and shares the authored tree; Agent Plugins 1.0.0 standardizes a portable core | Holds | WP-610 |
22	| 14 | Humans approve through written artifacts | specs, verdicts | The user asked for rendered examples repeatedly and drawn prototypes exposed defects the gated spec missed | Changing | WP-34, WP-614 |
23	| 15 | Agents use only `model` and `effort` of the host's controls | agent frontmatter | The host also offers `tools`, `maxTurns`, `isolation`, `skills` preload and `memory`; plugin agents ignore `hooks`, `mcpServers` and `permissionMode` | Open | WP-606 |
24	
25	## How to update
26	
27	Add a row when a decision record or architectural section introduces a new assumption. Change a status only with the evidence that moved it, citing a file in `docs/evaluations/` or a dated fact in `docs/verified-facts.md`. When a status becomes **Retire**, open or update the decision record that carries the assumption.

| 11 | Verification evidence is text, code and tests | `ARCHITECTURE.md` section 4 | Every target harness has a native browser; one study found 44.5% of agent runs never looked at the design screenshots; visible defects shipped past every gate | Changing | WP-607, WP-40, WP-41 |
| 12 | Agents are stateless across sessions | no memory design | Decisions were lost between sessions; native memory, persistent plugin data and session search exist | Changing | WP-612, WP-13 |
| 13 | Two source trees, one lifecycle contract | `ARCHITECTURE.md` sections 8 to 10 | Codex has its own native plugin format set up in `harnesses/codex/`; Antigravity's format is similar to Claude Code's and shares the authored tree; Agent Plugins 1.0.0 standardizes a portable core | Holds | WP-610 |
| 14 | Humans approve through written artifacts | specs, verdicts | The user asked for rendered examples repeatedly and drawn prototypes exposed defects the gated spec missed | Changing | WP-34, WP-614 |
| 15 | Agents use only `model` and `effort` of the host's controls | agent frontmatter | The host also offers `tools`, `maxTurns`, `isolation`, `skills` preload and `memory`; plugin agents ignore `hooks`, `mcpServers` and `permissionMode` | Open | WP-606 |

## How to update

Add a row when a decision record or architectural section introduces a new assumption. Change a status only with the evidence that moved it, citing a file in `docs/evaluations/` or a dated fact in `docs/verified-facts.md`. When a status becomes **Retire**, open or update the decision record that carries the assumption.

# VERIFY-4: What enters the context window

Date: 2026-11-07. Question: which sources put the most characters into the conversation, so that cuts go where they matter. Tool: `python3 tools/transcript-metrics.py context --match 'Projects-pages$|orin-dx-site'`. Sessions: the two audited projects. Characters, not tokens (divide by about 4). Each tool result is counted once; the model re-reads the whole context every turn, so an early large item costs more than its size.

## Result (16.2M characters)

| Origin | Characters | Share |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Tool results | 6.82M | 42% |
| Tool-call inputs (not delegation) | 6.02M | 37% |
| User text | 1.49M | 9% |
| Assistant text | 1.38M | 9% |
| Delegation prompts (`Agent`) | 0.46M | 3% |

Tool results by tool: Bash 77.5%, Artifact 10.0%, Read 3.6%, WebSearch 2.7%, Agent 2.1%, WebFetch 1.4%. Tool-call inputs by tool: Bash 4.44M, Write 0.66M, SendMessage 0.51M, Agent 0.46M, Workflow 0.14M, Read 0.12M.

## What it shows

- **Bash is about 60% of everything**: 5.28M characters of output and 4.44M of command text. The input side is long inline scripts and heredocs, which the earlier result-only measure (77% of results) hid. Cutting output alone reaches at most about 33% of the conversation; command text is the other half of the lever.
- **The five largest single results are `Artifact` reads of 50,000 to 56,000 characters each**: a read returns the whole published page. Reading a page back to confirm a publish, or to edit it, should be by path or a targeted diff, not the full HTML.
- **Delegation prompts are small (3%)**, and handoff results through `Agent` are 2% of results. The multi-agent plumbing is not the context cost; the work done in the main thread is.
- **`SendMessage` inputs (0.51M)** are as large as the delegation prompts: continuing agents with long messages.

## What it does not show

- Characters, not billed tokens, and no cache effect.
- Two projects, one author, and a period that included the unusual spec marathon; the shares will move on other work.
- It does not separate resident context (agent descriptions, skill bodies, memory), which is loaded every session and is measured statically: 45 agent descriptions about 6.9k tokens (`scripts/check-platform-limits.py`).

## Implications for the plugins

1. Skills that run commands should say to keep output short (filter, cap, show failing lines) and to write long scripts to a file, not inline.
2. Skills that publish artifacts should not read the page back whole.
3. The resident cost (descriptions, skill bodies) is a separate, static lever; the review-slop branch already cut descriptions by half and has not been ported here.

# ADR-003: Cognitive mode separation

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-08-08

## Context

Early plugin agents combined scanning and analysis in a single invocation — a single agent would grep for hazards and then assess whether each match was a real bug. This produced agents that were worse at both jobs: the scanner filtered matches because they "looked harmless," creating false negatives the downstream agent could never recover; the analyst had insufficient depth because it was also doing exhaustive enumeration. The alternative considered was one agent per cognitive mode.

## Decision

Agents are dispatched by the cognitive mode they require, not by pipeline position. Distinct modes: enumeration (mechanical completeness, no judgment — recon, scanner), tracing (systematic data-flow following — boundary-tracer), adversarial (default-to-skepticism, requires concrete failing scenario — adversary), systemic (cross-finding pattern recognition — architect), behavioral testing (tool execution and gap identification — mutator), judgment (weighing competing evidence for a binding decision — exit-gate, verifier), repair (minimum change + red-green verification — remediator, implementer). A plugin with multiple cognitive phases has a dedicated agent per mode. Model and effort tiers follow the same logic: `haiku/low` for enumeration, `sonnet/medium` for analysis, `opus/high` for binding judgment.

## Consequences

Each agent is optimized for exactly one cognitive mode and cannot self-corrupt by switching modes mid-task. A scanner cannot filter (its judgment criterion is "did you emit every match"); an adversary cannot enumerate (its judgment criterion is "can you state a concrete failing scenario"). Adding a new cognitive phase to a plugin always means a new agent file.
# ADR-009: Implementer may adapt the plan's code shape; task sizing is by compilation boundary, not clock time

**Status:** Accepted; the requirement that every task carry exact code is superseded by ADR-014 (plan code is now optional)
**Date:** 2026-09-01

## Context

Two related over-prescription patterns were identified on review:

1. `navigator`'s `planner` required "the exact implementation code" for every task, and `smith`'s `implementer` had no stated latitude to deviate from it — the plan effectively pre-decided the code's shape before the implementer, the agent with the most direct context on the actual codebase state at execution time, ever engaged. This is the same failure mode ADR-008 identified and fixed for test-write ordering (forcing a specific artifact into existence too early locks in a shape that is rarely revisited), applied one level higher in the pipeline, at a larger scale — a locked-in test is one assertion; locked-in "exact code" is the entire task. `navigator`'s own `challenger` already checks for a narrower version of this ("steps so rigid they leave no room to adapt" — its example is dictating private variable names), which shows the architecture already recognized over-prescription as a real failure mode, just scoped too narrowly to catch the structural version of it.

2. `planner` capped every task at "under fifteen minutes." `shared/agent-best-practices.md`'s own Subsystem Compilation Batching rule already argues against exactly this: "decompose plans by transactional crate/package compilation boundaries rather than arbitrary 15-minute intervals." The two rules were in direct tension. A clock-time estimate is also a human-ergonomics measure (a natural break point in a human working session) with no clear meaning for an agent that doesn't work in wall-clock sessions — the same category of mismatch ADR-008 found in TDD's red phase (a ritual calibrated to human psychology, not to what actually produces good agent output).

## Decision

**Implementer shape latitude:** `planner`'s exact implementation code is now explicitly a concrete baseline — proof that the task is achievable within its stated file targets and scope — not a transcript `implementer` must copy verbatim. `implementer` may use a better-shaped approach at execution time, provided it still satisfies the same file targets, `covers_criteria`, and tests the plan specified. Any such deviation is recorded in the `concerns` field, not silently applied and not silently withheld. The boundary is explicit: deviation is about implementation *shape* (how), never about *scope* (what) — a plan whose scope looks wrong is a `spec_contradiction` or `needs_architecture` case, not a quiet rewrite.

**Task sizing by compilation boundary, not clock time:** `planner` no longer sizes tasks by an estimated duration. A task must be one independently reviewable unit of change, sized to its Subsystem Batch's compilation boundary — the same criterion `agent-best-practices.md` already prescribed for batching, now applied consistently to task sizing itself rather than existing as a second, conflicting sizing rule.

## Consequences

`planner`'s plans remain fully concrete (no TBDs, no "implement as appropriate") — that discipline is unchanged and still exists for the same reason it always did: an unambiguous plan is what `challenger` can adversarially review and what prevents the original failure mode of implementer-invented scope decisions conflicting with the spec. What changes is narrower: the plan's code is a baseline whose *shape* is negotiable at execution time, while its *scope* (files, criteria, tests) remains binding. This does put more trust in `implementer`'s judgment than before — the countervailing control is that any deviation must be logged in `concerns`, giving `reviewer` and `exit-gate` a visible trail rather than an invisible one. Task sizing now has one consistent criterion (compilation-boundary cohesion) instead of two potentially conflicting ones (a batching rule and a per-task clock estimate), removing a standing inconsistency between `shared/agent-best-practices.md` and `navigator/agents/planner.md`.
# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Context

Every path through the plugins is gated: recon, a spec that may not contain a TBD, a binding exit gate, a plan, a challenger, then implementation with mutation, review and a second exit gate. That fits a contract many things depend on. It does not fit an idea nobody has seen yet.

Two real projects (the Orin DX and Techworx sites, September and October 2026) showed the cost. Eight component specs took 51 gate calls in under an hour, every one failed its first gate, and the retry cap of 3 was not enforced. The specs described behavior well and appearance not at all, so the owner asked for drawings and rewrote the gated specs the next day. On 14 October the owner asked for two phases, exploring quickly first and adding specs and tests once ideas narrow, and the audit machinery was stopped by hand; the landing, Tools and Principles pages then took about 30 minutes. Design ideation ran almost entirely outside the plugins: forks and general-purpose agents spent about 24.8 million subagent tokens, more than all the gates together, and decisions were lost between sessions. The plugin skills were also almost never invoked (7 Skill calls in 812 transcripts), so agents reachable only through skills never ran.

The evidence and the measurements are in `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/` (the transcript metrics, the unused-agents investigation and the verification notes). Industry practice points the same way: Vercel's product-design skill routes between a read-only shaping mode and a hardening mode, and Anthropic's own guidance says exploratory work may skip planning.

## Decision

Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.

- **`muse/sketch`** produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and a reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
- **`smith/spike`** produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works, with what was verified and what was not.
- **`muse/promote`** turns a chosen option or a working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
- Exploration modes are **non-binding**: no gate, no spec, no test requirement, open questions allowed. They write only to a scratch directory and to the artifact, mark the artifact `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, and stop before implementing. An exploration artifact is never evidence for a gate.
- Divergent generation, producing structurally different options without judging them, is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`), as ADR 003 requires for any new cognitive phase. Judging the options stays with the user.
- The modes and their rules live in one reference (`shared/references/architecture/modes.md`), loaded by the three skills. The skill is the entry point; its agents are internal.

## Options considered

- **Loosen the existing gates.** Rejected because the gates earn their cost on stable contracts: the SiteNav work passed 478 end-to-end tests, and loosening a gate for everyone weakens the cases that need it.
- **A light flag on each existing skill.** Rejected because one skill would carry two contracts, and the sessions show the orchestrator skipping skills it finds heavy; a separate, named, light skill is easier to choose and easier to evaluate.
- **A new plugin for exploration.** Deferred. `muse` is the only plugin that owns UI and design, and `AGENTS.md` lets one plugin hold several skills for heterogeneous intents. The artifact schema is UI-neutral so sketching can move into its own plugin if it is used outside UI work.
- **Leave exploration ad hoc.** Rejected: it produced the largest token cost, the lost decisions and the unreviewed visual defects.

## Consequences

There is now a named, light path for early work, and a stated way back into the gated pipeline. The risks are that an exploration artifact is mistaken for a spec, and that the light path is used where the gated path is needed. The `fidelity` marker, the promote-only rule, the list of cases that must use the full pipeline in `modes.md`, and the required note of which gates were skipped address them. Each new skill and agent needs its Codex counterpart; no plugin version or changelog changes until a release is cut. The new schemas follow ADR 004 and are immutable once published. Whether the light path is chosen when it should be, and whether it speeds exploration without raising the defects found later, is an open evaluation (see `docs/evaluation-methodology.md`).
# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Context

Every exit gate returns a `verdict@3` and is told to stop retrying after three attempts and hand the decision to a human. Both rules lived only in prompts. In the two audited projects, 12 of 45 recorded verdicts broke the schema (all 12 by a `verdict_summary` over 300 characters), and eight specs passed their gate with `retry_count` between 4 and 9. The `muse` gate was also told to emit a verdict value that no schema allows. A rule that matters in every run, and can be checked by a program, should not depend on a model remembering it.

Claude Code 2.1.271 and later deliver a subagent's report in auto mode through the `SubagentHandback` tool. A `PreToolUse` hook on that tool sees the report in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so the subagent can correct and hand back again. The platform checks were recorded in `docs/verified-facts.md`.

## Decision

Ship one stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, and register it in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) through `hooks/hooks.json`.

- It acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table and lets every other subagent through.
- It validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules.
- It denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth report passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- It enforces the retry cap in the report: a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with a blocker whose criterion is `escalation_required`.
- It fails open: an internal error never blocks a subagent.
- `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` appends one line per inspected report, for evaluation.

The prompts keep stating the rules, so harnesses without the hook still get the instruction. The hook is the enforcement where the host supports it.

## Options considered

- **Keep the rules in prompts.** Rejected: the recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill.** Rejected: the orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct its own output in place.
- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop.** Deferred to WP-603; it can replace the cap check later, but the schema check is useful either way.
- **Third-party JSON Schema library.** Rejected: hooks run on user machines with no install step. The validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, and a test covers each.

## Consequences

Gate conformance is checked on every run in Claude Code auto mode, and the retry cap can no longer be passed silently. Limits: the hook covers only the Claude Code host, only auto mode and only local, non-fork subagents; a hook failure or timeout does not block (`onFailure: "block"` needs Claude Code 2.1.295, and the local CLI is 2.1.292); plugin hooks fire for every subagent, so the routing table is the scope. Codex and Antigravity have no equivalent yet. A new gate agent needs a routing entry; a test enforces it. The validator supports a subset of JSON Schema, so a schema that adds keywords needs the validator extended in the same change. A live run on 2026-10-20 showed the hook denying twice and accepting the corrected third report from `muse:exit-gate`.
# ADR-013: Exit gates list the complete blocker set in round one and cite only known blockers on a retry

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10

## Context

In two real projects every spec failed its first gate. Blocker counts per round did not fall: SPEC-001 went 18, 5, 6, 0, 0, 2, 0, 6, 2, 3, 2, 8, 3 across 13 rounds, and eight specs passed only at `retry_count` 4 to 9. The muse gates cost about 8.15 million tokens over 79 calls (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/verification/VERIFY-3.md`, section 5; `CATALOG.md`, WP-50 and WP-212). A zero followed by a nonzero count means a later round found issues an earlier round could have found, or a fix broke something. Each extra round re-reads the whole artifact. ADR 012 already enforces schema conformance and the retry cap by hook, but not round discipline.

## Decision

- Each exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) states two rules in its `<output>` section, worded the same in all five. In round one (`retry_count` 0 or absent) it lists the complete blocker set. On a retry it cites only blockers from the prior round that remain unresolved, or regressions the fix introduced; any other newly noticed issue is a `coverage_gaps` entry with `blocking: false`.
- A blocker names the criterion or section in `criterion`, cites evidence (quoted text or a location) in `finding`, and states the exact change required. A wording-only or style-only issue is a note, never a blocker.
- The drafters that feed a spec gate (`muse:drafter`, `scribe:drafter`) load `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` and check their draft against its spec checklist before returning. The checklist and blocker wording live in that one reference.
- `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py` additionally denies a blocker or coverage gap whose text field is only whitespace. It checks nothing else about blocker content.

Gates stay default-fail and adversarial; no pass condition is relaxed. `verdict@3` is unchanged.

## Options considered

- **A `verdict@4` with a `regression` or `prior_blocker_id` field on each blocker.** Rejected for now: `verdict@3` already expresses the rule through `blockers` and `coverage_gaps`, and ADR 004 makes a new schema version costly. Revisit if WP-212 needs the hook to tell fix-induced blockers from late-found ones; today the hook cannot, because a retry is a new subagent with no stored prior verdict.
- **Hook checks that a blocker has a `location`, a minimum length, or a quote.** Rejected: an `escalation_required` or `missing_mutation_gate` blocker has no location, and a terse correct blocker would be denied. Each denial costs a turn. Only blank text is rejected.
- **Make the gate lenient on retries (accept anything not previously listed).** Rejected as stated; the rule does not drop findings, it records them as non-blocking gaps the orchestrator sees.
- **Put the rule in the shared constitution.** Rejected: the constitution block is copied byte for byte into every agent (ADR 006), so any change touches all 40 agents; the rule applies only to gates.

## Consequences

Expected: fewer rounds and fewer tokens per gated spec, with the same defects caught. Not yet measured; a live run (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`) confirms the hook fires and the gates run, not that rounds fall. Costs: a defect a gate misses in round one can now pass as a non-blocking gap on a retry, so the gap list needs a reader; and a gate can only tell a retry from round one if the orchestrator supplies `retry_count` and the prior blockers, which the skills do not yet pass. The skills track must carry the prior blockers into the retry input.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (blank text), `tests/test_agent_structure.py` and `tests/test_prompt_alignment.py` (agent shape). The round rules themselves are prompt rules.
# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10
**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.

## Context

ADR-009 made the plan's exact implementation code a baseline the implementer may reshape, and kept the plan fully concrete so `challenger` has something to review. The baseline was still required for every task, so `planner` wrote a body for every function, `challenger` policed it, and `implementer` was told not to copy it. The planner prompt was the second-largest agent file.

Three observations argue against writing code for every task. Plans of 60 to 130 KB stalled agents in the audited projects (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/ARCHITECTURE-REVIEW.md`, assumption 10). Anthropic's guidance says instructions written for earlier models are often too prescriptive for current ones and reduce output quality, and its own planner stays at high-level design. And a body the implementer is told it may discard buys little: the guardrail ADR-009 wanted is the plan's scope (files, signatures, tests, criteria), which does not need the body.

`plan@1` does not require code. A task requires `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` (an array of strings), and `commit_message`; "exact code" appears only in a field description, and `additionalProperties` is false, so every part of a task other than those fields lives in `steps` strings.

## Decision

`planner` writes each task as an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`. It adds implementation code only where the logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape would be costly to undo: ordering or concurrency rules, numeric or parsing edge cases, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, algorithms the spec states only by result, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.

`challenger` flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified`, and treats a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`. It no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its checks for missing work, ordering, criterion coverage and sibling interfaces are unchanged.

No schema change. `plan@1` stays as published (ADR-004). The shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer that reads a plan (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already handles free-text steps.

## Options considered

- **Keep exact code for every task.** Rejected: it is the cost this record exists to cut, and ADR-009 already made the code non-binding.
- **Drop code entirely.** Rejected: a wrong shape in a wire format, a parsing edge or a cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent, and weaker implementers lose a guardrail.
- **A plan mode (outcome-level or full-code) chosen per run.** Rejected: it doubles the planner and challenger surface to test, and a per-task rule already covers both ends.
- **A `plan@2` with explicit outcome, signature and test fields.** Rejected for now: the existing `steps` array carries the content, and a new version would need every consumer and the pipeline fixtures to move. Revisit if consumers need to read the fields programmatically.
- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code.** Rejected: a published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004). The descriptions are stale but harmless.

## Consequences

Plans are smaller. One run on a six-criterion fixture produced a plan 43% smaller in characters with every criterion still covered (see `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`). Whether implementers do better or worse with outcome-level plans is untested. The risks are that an implementer in a weaker model invents a wrong shape where the plan gave only a signature, and that a plan with no code is harder for `challenger` to falsify. The rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call the planner can get wrong in either direction.

ADR-009 stays Accepted as to implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; only its requirement that every task carry the exact code is superseded. Its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_navigator_plan.py` checks the planner and challenger rules, the unchanged schema, and that a plan in the new shape validates against `plan@1`.
